Baby & Child

Is your family ready for a pet?

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Before bringing an animal home, picture an ordinary Tuesday. Your child has a fever, you are late for work, and the water bowl is empty. Who fills it? The answer matters more to the animal than a promise made on the day you meet. It also gives your family a place to start talking about what life with a pet would really be like.

Find out what your child is hoping for

Ask your child to describe an afternoon with the animal they have in mind. One child imagines a dog that greets them after school. Another wants to watch a fish explore a tank. Someone who likes the idea of a cat may feel nervous when one actually comes close. Listen to those differences. Offer a supervised visit with a suitable animal and let your child watch from a distance if they prefer.

A relationship with a pet can give a particular child comfort, pleasure and chances to practise being gentle. Families sometimes hope it will also lift persistent low mood. A UK study that followed children over time found little evidence of a link between pet ownership and better emotional health after accounting for differences between families. If your child is struggling, seek help for that difficulty on its own terms. Adoption is a separate family decision.

Give the child a real job and the adult a backup plan

Choose one task you can do together. A child might help fill the water bowl while an adult checks that fresh water is always available. An older child might help a caregiver note what the pet ate, or tell them when an animal is hiding more than usual. A chart can show who did a job and when. It works best when everyone knows which adult will check it.

If your child forgets, meet the animal’s need straight away. Talk later about what made the job hard. Was the food stored too high? Did an evening activity change the routine? You can shorten the task or make it a shared job again. Adults remain responsible for feeding, a safe home, hygiene, veterinary care and arranging cover during illness or travel.

Choose an animal your household can actually care for

Consider space, housing rules, costs, noise, lifespan and the animal’s daily needs. A small animal can require specialist equipment and years of care. Ask a veterinarian or an experienced shelter worker about the individual animal’s temperament and handling needs. Give every member of the household a chance to voice fears or concerns about allergies before deciding.

Age and health affect the choice. Reptiles and amphibians, including turtles and frogs, can carry Salmonella even when they look healthy. CDC advises families with children under five or people with weakened immune systems to choose a different pet. A tank adds surfaces and water that can carry germs. An adult should assess these needs before bringing an animal home.

Teach the child to notice when the animal wants space

Watch a calm animal together. If it walks away or hides, help your child let it go. Give a pet a resting place where a child will leave it alone. An adult should be close enough to intervene when a young child is with an animal, even a familiar one. Children can enjoy watching an animal without picking it up, hugging it or bringing their face close.

Wash hands with soap and running water after touching the pet, its food, bowl or habitat. Help a younger child do this well. Keep animal supplies away from areas where the family prepares food. Ask a veterinarian how to clean the animal’s space safely and which tasks an adult should handle. These habits belong in the plan from day one.

Talk honestly when a pet is sick or dies

Tell a child what has happened in simple words. For example, “Milo died today. His body stopped working, and he can’t come home.” Pause for the child’s question. A young child may ask tomorrow if the pet is coming back. Answer gently again. If the child wonders whether missing one routine caused the death, explain what you know and address the guilt directly.

A child might want to draw a favourite moment, share a photograph, sit quietly with you or play as usual for a while. Make room for those different responses. Before discussing another pet, ask what your child misses about this one. If grief is overwhelming or keeps a child from sleeping, attending school or managing everyday life, contact their healthcare professional.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Have an adult plan for every essential task, including veterinary care and travel cover.

Supervise children around pets and build handwashing into the routine.

Persistent emotional distress deserves attention regardless of pet ownership.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests planning one ordinary day with the animal so a family can weigh the child’s wishes alongside the animal’s long-term needs.

When to seek help

A healthy-looking animal can carry germs. Ask a veterinarian about a suitable pet and speak with your clinician about household allergies or a weakened immune system.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Name the adult responsible for each essential care task before choosing a pet.
  • Offer a child a small supervised role and adjust it as their skills develop.
  • Consider the specific animal, the youngest household member and anyone at higher risk from infection.
  • Use direct, gentle words when a pet dies and make room for repeated questions.

Frequently asked questions

Can a pet improve my child’s mental health?

A child may find companionship with an animal meaningful. Research has not shown that simply adopting a pet reliably improves children’s emotional health. Discuss persistent sadness, withdrawal or anxiety with a healthcare professional, whether or not the family has a pet.

What can my child learn by caring for an animal?

A modest job gives your child a chance to pay attention to another living thing. Filling a water bowl alongside an adult, noticing when a pet needs space or remembering a shared routine can all be useful. An adult checks that the care actually happens.

Which pet is best for a child?

Start with your child’s interest, then investigate what the whole household can provide. Consider temperament, lifespan, costs, supervision and health risks. A small size does not guarantee simple care. Families with children under five should avoid reptiles and amphibians.

What if my child wants an animal but we cannot keep one?

A supervised visit with a familiar, suitable animal can help you learn what your child enjoys. Some children prefer drawing animals or observing them from a distance. It is reasonable to wait until an adult has the time and resources for the animal’s full care.

How can I help my child after our pet dies?

Say plainly that the animal died, answer questions and offer chances to remember it in the child’s own way. A child may return to a question after a day of ordinary play. Seek support if grief is making everyday activities consistently difficult.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
